comment: I overextended K1114’s polynomial high-rate caution to a cross-optimizer comparison. D beating C does not imply RMSprop A also beats C. C’s tenfold higher learning rate plausibly provided enough fitting progress to outperform A despite worse late precision than D; the ordinal result does not identify that mechanism. K1001/K1012 warned against this extrapolation, while K1003/K1019 supported placing the slow SGD candidates last. Backtesting supports C over A, but lab coverage does not match this deep normalized network.
hypothesis:
For multivariate symbolic MSE on [0,1]^n, identical MLPs and training budgets of 256–1024 steps, prefer Adam/AdamW over RMSprop when lr_Adam/lr_RMSprop ≥3. This is a pairwise preference, not a maximum-rate rule or a complete ranking.

History backtest, excluding the focal question: 32 eligible comparisons across 19 questions, 32 hits and 0 misses. Including two 2048-step comparisons gives 34/34 across 21 questions. Optimizer decay and betas may differ.

Lab backtest with identical model/loss within each set and zero reported failures: 16/16 comparisons favor the higher-rate Adam-family candidate across four sets, all at T256 and using shallow width16 residual GELU networks. At exactly Adam .003 versus RMSprop .0003, results are 8/8. These dependent comparisons provide no matched deep-network replication. Equal-rate comparisons reverse the preference: Adam-family wins only 10/42 lab pairs and 4/16 history pairs.

Proposed mechanism: the higher Adam-family rate outweighs RMSprop’s early adaptation advantage. Actual updates were not measured. The rule predicts C<A here without predicting C<D; its deep-network transfer remains falsifiable.
